title: HTTP Authentication: Field Notes
summary: A dense study-notes carousel covering how HTTP authentication actually works: Basic auth, Bearer tokens, HMAC request signing, API keys vs tokens, the 401/403 split, and the WWW-Authenticate header that drives it all.

chapters.title: 1. Authentication Fundamentals
points: Authentication = proving WHO you are; authorization = deciding WHAT you may do — HTTP conflates them in one header: Authorization
The Authorization header: 'Authorization: <scheme> <credentials>' — scheme token tells the server how to interpret the rest
Common scheme names: Basic, Bearer, Digest, HOBA, plus custom ones like 'Token' or 'HMAC-SHA256'
401 Unauthorized is misleadingly named — it really means 'Unauthenticated': your identity was not established
RFC 7235 defines the framework (challenge/response); RFC 7617 defines Basic, RFC 6750 defines Bearer
Challenge-response flow: client sends request → server replies 401 + WWW-Authenticate → client retries with credentials
Proxies have their own pair: Proxy-Authenticate / Proxy-Authorization with status 407
Transport security is a prerequisite: any credential sent over plain HTTP is readable by anyone on the path
Servers usually read auth from the header, but many APIs also accept ?api_key= or cookies — query strings leak into logs
Stateless HTTP: every request must re-present credentials unless you layer sessions/cookies on top
Auth headers are typically added per request by clients, interceptors, or gateway middleware
Rule of thumb: never roll your own credential format when a standard scheme fits

chapters.title: 2. WWW-Authenticate: The Challenge Header
points: Response header, not request header: server → client, announcing accepted schemes and how to join
Shape: 'WWW-Authenticate: <scheme> realm="...", <params>' — e.g. Basic realm="Admin Panel"
realm is a human-readable label shown in browser login prompts; it also scopes credentials per protection space
Multiple challenges allowed: 'WWW-Authenticate: Bearer, Basic realm="api"' — client picks the strongest it supports
Bearer challenges carry error info (RFC 6750): error="invalid_token", error_description="token expired"
Digest challenges include nonce, qop, opaque, algorithm — parameters the client must echo into its response hash
Browsers react to Basic challenges with a native popup; API clients should NOT — a JSON API returning a browser popup is a UX smell
Always pair a 401 with WWW-Authenticate (RFC says it's required); 403 must NOT include it
Caching gotcha: 401 responses are cacheable unless explicitly prevented — add Cache-Control: no-store
Inspecting WWW-Authenticate with curl -v is the fastest way to learn what a protected endpoint expects
Some frameworks misconfigure this: returning 401 with no challenge breaks clients that retry correctly
Custom schemes still use this header: 'WWW-Authenticate: HMAC-SHA256 realm="api"'

chapters.title: 3. Basic Auth: Mechanics & Pitfalls
points: Basic auth = username:password encoded with Base64, NOT encrypted: 'Authorization: Basic dXNlcjpwYXNz'
Base64 is reversible encoding, zero secrecy — decode with `echo dXNlcjpwYXNz | base64 -d`
Full flow: request → 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm=... → browser popup → retry with encoded credentials
Credentials are re-sent on EVERY request — there is no logout, only browser-tab close or credential invalidation
Colon in username is illegal as separator: 'user:na:me:pass' parses as username 'user', password 'na:me:pass'
Charset pitfalls: non-ASCII passwords need RFC 7617 charset="UTF-8" param, or behavior is undefined
Server side: compare hashes (bcrypt/argon2), never plaintext; beware timing attacks — use constant-time compare
Legit uses: quick internal tools, curl prototyping, sub-protected staging behind TLS, basic proxies
Bad uses: public APIs, mobile apps (credentials baked in = stolen), anything needing per-scope permissions
No expiry, no revocation granularity, no scopes, no MFA support — one leaked header = full account
Mitigation if forced to use it: TLS only, IP allowlists, rate limiting on auth failures, strong random passwords
curl example: `curl -u alice:s3cret https://api.example.com/me` sets the header for you
Digest auth was the historical upgrade (hash challenge instead of plaintext) — now deprecated territory; prefer tokens

chapters.title: 4. Bearer Tokens & OAuth 2.0
points: Bearer = 'whoever bears this token gets access' — the token itself IS the credential, no signature to present
Typical shape: opaque random string or a JWT: 'Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...' three dot-separated base64url parts
JWT anatomy: header {alg,typ} . payload {sub, exp, scope...} . signature — payload is readable by anyone, just not forgeable
Never put secrets in a JWT payload; it's Base64url, not encryption — use JWE or keep secrets server-side
Validate JWTs fully: signature, exp, nbf, iss, aud, and algorithm (reject 'alg: none' and algorithm-confusion attacks)
OAuth 2.0 is the delegation framework that issues Bearer tokens: grant types = authorization_code (web apps), client_credentials (machine-to-machine), refresh_token
Token lifetimes: short-lived access tokens (minutes) + long-lived refresh tokens = blast-radius control
Storage matters: browsers → httpOnly cookies or memory; localStorage is XSS-readable; servers → secrets manager, never git
Revocation: opaque tokens are trivially revocable at the auth server; JWTs are valid until exp unless you add a denylist or short TTL
RFC 6750 sender-constrained tokens: DPoP / mTLS bind a token to a key so a stolen token can't be replayed
curl example: `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://api.example.com/me`
Common bug: pasting the token with the word 'Bearer' already inside the env var → 'Bearer Bearer xyz' 401

chapters.title: 5. HMAC Request Signing
points: HMAC = Hash-based Message Authentication Code: keyed hash proving both authenticity AND integrity of the request
Core idea: signature = HMAC-SHA256(secret, canonical_string_of_request) — sent alongside, e.g. 'Authorization: HMAC-SHA256 ...' or X-Signature header
Canonical string typically includes: method, path, sorted query params, headers like host/date/content-type, and a SHA-256 of the body
The secret never travels the wire — only the signature does; server recomputes and constant-time compares
Replay protection: include a timestamp (+/- 5 min window) and/or nonce; AWS SigV4 adds 'X-Amz-Date' plus scope for this
AWS SigV4 is the reference implementation: canonical request → string-to-sign → signing key derived from secret + date/region/service → final signature
Body must be hashed into the signature, or attackers can swap your JSON payload while keeping a valid signature
Why HMAC over Bearer for machine-to-machine: nothing bearer-like to steal, request is tamper-proof, no token expiry churn
Costs: harder client integration, clock-skew failures ('Signature expired'), every middleware touching the request can break signing
Debugging recipe: log canonical string on both sides — 99% of failures are byte-level mismatch (trailing newline, unsorted params, different casing)
curl sketch: `SIG=$(echo -n "$CANONICAL" | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "$SECRET")` then attach X-Signature
Gotcha: proxies/load balancers rewriting Host or Date headers invalidate signatures — sign only headers you control
Constant-time comparison (hmac.compare_digest) prevents timing attacks on signature verification

chapters.title: 6. API Keys vs Tokens
points: API key = static identifier string, often just proof that 'this app is calling'; token = dynamic credential representing a subject + permissions
API keys usually travel as headers (X-API-Key) or query params; tokens use the Authorization: Bearer scheme
Semantic difference: key identifies an application or project; token identifies a user/session or a scoped delegation
API keys: no expiry by default, no standard refresh, no scopes (or coarse ones), revocation = regenerate and redeploy
Tokens: expiration, refresh, fine-grained scopes (read:orders), and standardized issuance via OAuth
Rate limiting and billing are the real jobs of API keys — authn for humans is not
Baking an API key into frontend JavaScript = publishing it; use a backend proxy or token-exchange pattern instead
Hybrid pattern: API key identifies the client app + Bearer token identifies the acting user — many real APIs require both
Rotation story: keys are painful to rotate (outages, redeploy); tokens rotate invisibly via refresh flow
Leak handling: leaked token dies at exp; leaked key lives until you notice — scan repos with secret-scanning tooling
Use keys for server-to-server telemetry/quotas; use tokens whenever user identity or least-privilege matters
Never send API keys in query strings — they end up in server logs, browser history, and referrer headers

chapters.title: 7. 401 vs 403: Who Are You vs May You
points: 401 Unauthorized = 'I don't know who you are' — authentication failed or missing; fixable by sending valid credentials
403 Forbidden = 'I know exactly who you are, and you can't do this' — authorization failed; retrying won't help
Hard rule: 401 responses SHOULD include WWW-Authenticate; 403 responses MUST NOT
Decide with one question: 'Would sending different credentials change the outcome?' yes → 401, no → 403
Examples of 401: missing Authorization header, expired token, bad signature, malformed Basic encoding
Examples of 403: valid user lacking 'admin' role, token scope 'read' hitting a write endpoint, IP/geo blocked for an authenticated user
404-instead-of-403 pattern: hide existence of resources from unauthorized eyes to avoid enumeration leaks
Security smell: returning 403 for expired tokens lets attackers map valid tokens — use 401 for credential-validity failures
Client behavior: on 401 → refresh token or re-authenticate once; on 403 → show access-denied UI, don't retry
Related statuses: 407 (proxy needs auth), 407+Proxy-Authenticate mirrors the 401 flow through proxies
Some APIs hide all failures as generic 401/403 messages to avoid leaking which emails or endpoints exist — deliberate opacity is fine
Common bug: framework default returns 403 for unauthenticated requests (Spring Security, Django defaults vary) — audit your error mapping

chapters.title: 8. Security Trade-offs & Threat Model
points: TLS is non-negotiable: Basic auth, Bearer tokens, and API keys are all plaintext credentials once on the wire
Attack surfaces: credential stuffing, replay attacks, token theft via XSS, key leakage via logs and referrer, MITM without TLS
Blast radius ranking (best→worst): HMAC signed request < short-lived scoped Bearer < long-lived Bearer < static API key < Basic auth
HMAC defeats replay/tamper but costs integration complexity and clock sync; Bearer trades security for universal simplicity
Scopes = least privilege: a token that can only 'read:orders' limits damage even when stolen
Token lifetime vs revocation trade-off: short TTL + denylist gives both, but adds infrastructure (auth server checks)
Constant-time comparisons everywhere: password hashes, API keys, signatures — timing attacks recover secrets byte-by-byte
Rate-limit and lock out on auth failures; standardize on 401 with WWW-Authenticate so clients can back off
Logging discipline: redact Authorization headers, mask keys (show last 4 chars), never log full tokens even in debug
Secrets in code/repos are the #1 real-world leak — use env vars, secret managers, and pre-commit secret scanning
MFA and passwordless (WebAuthn/passkeys) sit above all these schemes for human login — use OAuth/OIDC to bridge into API auth
Defense in depth: combine schemes — API key for app identity + Bearer for user + HMAC for sensitive money-moving endpoints

chapters.title: 9. Practical Playbook
points: Choosing a scheme: human sessions → OAuth/OIDC + Bearer; server-to-server → mTLS, OAuth client_credentials, or HMAC; quotas/analytics → API key
Debugging 401s, step 1: `curl -v` and read the WWW-Authenticate header — it literally tells you what the server wants
Step 2: verify header formatting — exact scheme casing, single space, no quotes around the token, no CRLF/whitespace from env vars
Step 3: check clock skew for HMAC (NTP) and expiry for JWTs; decode JWT payload with jwt.io to inspect exp/aud/iss
Client implementation: attach auth via an interceptor/middleware so every request gets it consistently; handle 401 with one refresh-and-retry
Never implement Basic auth login pages yourself in browsers — the native popup has no logout, no MFA, no password reset UX
Server checklist: require TLS, reject 'alg: none' JWTs, constant-time compares, rate-limit failures, return correct 401/403 + challenge
Versioning and deprecation: when rotating schemes, keep WWW-Authenticate advertising the accepted set so clients can migrate
Testing: unit-test auth middleware with expired/missing/wrong-scope credentials; fuzz Authorization header parsing (malformed encodings cause 500s)
Observability: log auth events (success/failure/scheme) with request IDs — failed-auth spikes are your first breach signal
Documentation pattern for APIs: show the exact curl with -H "Authorization: Bearer ..." and one 401 and one 403 example response
Golden rule: standard schemes + TLS + least-privilege scopes beats any clever homemade auth design

chapters.title: 10. Cheat Sheet & Summary
points: One-line map: Basic = Base64 user:pass · Bearer = portable token · HMAC = signed request · API key = app identifier
Flow to memorize: request → 401 + WWW-Authenticate → credentials → 200, or valid-credentials-but-denied → 403 (no challenge)
Authorization header anatomy: 'Scheme' + space + credentials; response twin is WWW-Authenticate; proxy twins are Proxy-Authenticate/Proxy-Authorization (407)
Basic auth: only with TLS, only for demos/internal — no logout, no scopes, no revocation
Bearer: short-lived access + refresh, validate signature + exp + iss + aud, never trust payload contents as secrets
HMAC: sign method+path+headers+body-hash, add timestamp/nonce for replay defense, compare in constant time
API key vs token: key = who the APP is (quotas, billing); token = who the USER is and what scope was delegated
401 vs 403 decision: would new credentials change the answer? yes → 401, no → 403
Top mistakes recap: secrets in query strings, localStorage token storage, 'alg: none', Base64 mistaken for encryption, 403/401 swapped
Top mistakes recap 2: forgetting WWW-Authenticate on 401, logging Authorization headers, signing headers that proxies rewrite
Escalation path for humans: passwords → MFA → passkeys (WebAuthn), then OAuth/OIDC issues the API tokens — don't hand-roll
Final exam question: a request with a valid, unexpired token hits an admin endpoint and the user lacks the role — status? Answer: 403, no WWW-Authenticate
